problems.text: A 12-pack of juice boxes costs $4.68. What is the cost of one juice box (in dollars)?
hints: You want the cost for ONE box. What do you divide by?
Get to ONE: divide the total cost by the number of boxes.
steps: 'Per box' means divide by the 12 boxes.
problems.why_focus: Practice getting to ONE, the move every other problem in this unit uses.

problems.text: Brand X: 18 oz for $5.04. Brand Y: 30 oz for $8.10. Which costs less per ounce?
hints: Compare the cost of ONE ounce for each brand.
Divide each price by its ounces.
steps: The smaller price per ounce is the better deal.
problems.why_focus: Practice getting to ONE, the move every other problem in this unit uses.

problems.text: A printer prints 84 pages in 6 minutes. At that rate, how many pages in 25 minutes?
hints: First, how many pages in ONE minute?
problems.why_focus: Practice getting to ONE, the move every other problem in this unit uses.

problems.text: A class has 4 boys for every 5 girls. There are 35 girls. How many boys?
hints: Make a ratio table: boys on one row, girls on the other.
How do you get from 5 girls to 35 girls?
Do the same to the 4 boys.
steps: 5 × 7 = 35, so multiply the boys by 7 too.
problems.why_focus: Practice getting to ONE, the move every other problem in this unit uses.

problems.text: A recipe uses 3 cups of flour for every 12 muffins. Flour costs $0.40 per cup. What does the flour cost for 60 muffins (in dollars)?
hints: Two steps: cups of flour first, then cost.
60 muffins is 5 times as many as 12 muffins.
problems.why_focus: Practice getting to ONE, the move every other problem in this unit uses.

problems.text: Gloves are sold 3 dozen for $54. What does one pair cost (in dollars)?
hints: How many single pairs are in 3 dozen?
problems.why_focus: Practice getting to ONE, the move every other problem in this unit uses.

problems.text: Ava types 195 words in 5 minutes. Ben types 224 words in 7 minutes. Who types faster?
hints: Faster means more words in ONE minute.
Divide words by minutes for each person.
steps: More words per minute is faster.
problems.why_focus: Practice getting to ONE, the move every other problem in this unit uses.

problems.text: A hose fills 3/4 of a bucket in 1/2 minute. How many buckets per minute?
hints: Per minute: what has to be 1?
problems.why_focus: Practice keep-change-flip to get to ONE when the amounts are fractions.

problems.text: A cyclist rides 5/6 mile in 1/12 hour. What is the speed in miles per hour?
hints: Miles per hour: hours go on the bottom.
problems.why_focus: Practice keep-change-flip to get to ONE when the amounts are fractions.

problems.text: There are 120 Calories in 2/3 cup of cereal. How many Calories are in 2 cups?
problems.why_focus: Practice keep-change-flip to get to ONE when the amounts are fractions.

problems.text: Runner A goes 1 1/2 miles in 1/4 hour. Runner B goes 2 1/4 miles in 1/3 hour. Who is faster?
hints: Find miles per ONE hour for each runner.
Turn mixed numbers into fractions: 3/2 and 9/4.
problems.why_focus: Practice keep-change-flip to get to ONE when the amounts are fractions.

problems.text: On a map, 3/8 inch = 6 miles. How many real miles is 2 1/4 inches on the map?
hints: Find miles for ONE inch first.
problems.why_focus: Practice keep-change-flip to get to ONE when the amounts are fractions.

problems.text: A machine makes 5 parts in 2/3 hour. How many hours does ONE part take? (Fraction or decimal.)
hints: Hours per part: parts go on the bottom.
steps: = 2/15 of an hour (about 0.13 hour, or 8 minutes).
problems.why_focus: Practice keep-change-flip to get to ONE when the amounts are fractions.

problems.text: Is the relationship between x and y proportional?
hints: Divide y ÷ x in EVERY column.
steps: Every row gives 3.5, so it is proportional (k = 3.5).
problems.why_focus: Practice testing EVERY row so a broken pattern can't fool you.

problems.text: Is the relationship between x and y proportional?
hints: Divide y ÷ x in EVERY column, including the last.
steps: The last column breaks the pattern, so it is NOT proportional.
problems.why_focus: Practice testing EVERY row so a broken pattern can't fool you.

problems.text: This table is proportional. What is y when x = 8?
problems.why_focus: Practice testing EVERY row so a broken pattern can't fool you.

problems.text: A game center charges $4 to get in plus $3 per game. The cost for 1, 2, 3 games is $7, $10, $13. Is the cost proportional to the number of games?
steps: Also, 0 games still costs $4. A starting fee means NOT proportional.
problems.why_focus: Practice testing EVERY row so a broken pattern can't fool you.

problems.text: This table is proportional. What is y when x = 5?
hints: Find y ÷ x using a column.
problems.why_focus: Practice testing EVERY row so a broken pattern can't fool you.

problems.text: Which table is proportional?
hints: Check y ÷ x for each table.
problems.why_focus: Practice testing EVERY row so a broken pattern can't fool you.

problems.text: A hiker walks 14 miles in 4 hours at a steady pace. What is the constant of proportionality k (miles per hour)?
hints: k is y over x. What is y here, and what is x?
problems.why_focus: Practice finding k and using y = kx to find any amount.

problems.text: y = 6.5x. What is y when x = 14?
problems.why_focus: Practice finding k and using y = kx to find any amount.

problems.text: y = 0.4x. What is x when y = 18?
problems.why_focus: Practice finding k and using y = kx to find any amount.

problems.text: For every 5 tickets, the cost goes up $32.50. What is the cost of ONE ticket (that's k)?
hints: Is $32.50 the price of one ticket?
problems.why_focus: Practice finding k and using y = kx to find any amount.

problems.text: Tickets cost $6.50 each. The equation is y = 6.5x. What do 12 tickets cost (in dollars)?
problems.why_focus: Practice finding k and using y = kx to find any amount.

problems.text: Which equation shows a proportional relationship?
hints: A proportional equation is exactly y = (number) × x.
Look for a plus or minus.
steps: y = 4x + 1 and y = x + 4 add a number, so no.
y = 4/x has x on the bottom, so no.
y = 0.4x is y = kx with k = 0.4.
problems.why_focus: Practice finding k and using y = kx to find any amount.

problems.text: A pool fills 45 gallons in 1.5 minutes at a steady rate. How many gallons in 8 minutes?
hints: Find gallons per ONE minute first.
problems.why_focus: Practice finding k and using y = kx to find any amount.

problems.text: Is this graph a proportional relationship?
hints: Two tests: is it straight? Does it go through (0, 0)?
Look at where the line starts.
It starts at the origin and it's straight.
steps: Both tests pass, so it is proportional.
problems.why_focus: Practice the two graph tests: straight, and through (0, 0).

problems.text: Use the same graph. What is the constant of proportionality k?
hints: k = y ÷ x for any point except (0, 0).
The point (4, 10) is on the line.
steps: k = 2.5, so the point (1, 2.5) is also on the line.
problems.why_focus: Practice the two graph tests: straight, and through (0, 0).

problems.text: Is this graph a proportional relationship?
hints: Where does the line cross the y-axis?
steps: The line is straight, but it starts at (0, 3).
It does not pass through the origin, so it is NOT proportional.
problems.why_focus: Practice the two graph tests: straight, and through (0, 0).

problems.text: Is this graph a proportional relationship?
hints: It does pass through (0, 0). Is it straight?
steps: It passes through (0, 0), but it is a curve, not a straight line.
Both tests must pass. So it is NOT proportional.
problems.why_focus: Practice the two graph tests: straight, and through (0, 0).

problems.text: A proportional graph is a straight line through (0, 0) and (5, 35). What is y when x = 1?
hints: The point (1, k) shows the constant of proportionality.
steps: So the point is (1, 7), and y = 7 when x = 1.
problems.why_focus: Practice the two graph tests: straight, and through (0, 0).

problems.text: Two proportional graphs, Line A and Line B, both start at (0, 0). Which line has the bigger constant of proportionality k?
hints: Find k for each: y ÷ x at the end point.
A ends at (4, 6) and B ends at (4, 10).
steps: The steeper line has the bigger k.
problems.why_focus: Practice the two graph tests: straight, and through (0, 0).

problems.text: Mia is 4 years old when her cousin is 10. How old will her cousin be when Mia is 9?
hints: Times or plus? Will they ever be the same age gap apart?
Their ages keep a constant DIFFERENCE.
The cousin is always 6 years older.
steps: Mia's age + 6 = cousin's age (a plus, not a times).
This is NOT a proportional problem.
problems.why_focus: Practice deciding times or plus BEFORE you calculate.

problems.text: 4 people paint a fence in 6 hours. How many hours would 8 people take, working at the same rate?
hints: More people: more time, or less time?
Total work stays the same: 4 × 6 = 24 person-hours.
steps: More helpers means LESS time, so this is not a simple ratio.
problems.why_focus: Practice deciding times or plus BEFORE you calculate.

problems.text: A smoothie uses 2 cups of berries for every 3 cups of yogurt. You use 15 cups of yogurt. How many cups of berries?
hints: Times or plus? Doubling the recipe doubles both.
How many groups of 3 cups of yogurt are in 15?
problems.why_focus: Practice deciding times or plus BEFORE you calculate.

problems.text: Trail mix should have 4 cups of nuts for every 7 cups of raisins. A bag has 12 cups of nuts and 28 cups of raisins. How many MORE cups of nuts does it need?
hints: Match the ratio to the bigger amount of raisins.
steps: 28 ÷ 7 = 4 groups, so the mix needs 4 × 4 = 16 cups of nuts.
It has 12, so it needs 16 − 12 = 4 more.
problems.why_focus: Practice deciding times or plus BEFORE you calculate.

problems.text: 30 inches of ribbon cost $4.50. How much do 3 yards cost (in dollars)? (1 yard = 36 inches)
problems.why_focus: Practice deciding times or plus BEFORE you calculate.

problems.text: A taxi charges $5 plus $2 per mile. Is the cost proportional to the number of miles?
hints: Check cost ÷ miles for 1 and 2 miles.
steps: There is a $5 starting fee, so it is NOT proportional.
problems.why_focus: Practice deciding times or plus BEFORE you calculate.

problems.text: Scale: 1 in. = 4 ft. A wall measures 7.5 in. on the drawing. How many feet long is the real wall?
hints: Does the real wall come out bigger or smaller than the drawing?
problems.why_focus: Practice using the scale, and converting each side before finding area.

problems.text: Scale: 2 in. = 9 ft. A room is 5 in. long on the drawing. How many feet long is the real room?
hints: First make the scale 'ONE inch = ? ft'.
problems.why_focus: Practice using the scale, and converting each side before finding area.

problems.text: A drawing of a rectangle is 3 in. by 5 in. Scale: 1 in. = 6 ft. What is the REAL area in square feet?
hints: Do not multiply the drawing's area by 6.
Find the real length and the real width first.
steps: Real width: 3 × 6 = 18 ft. Real length: 5 × 6 = 30 ft.
problems.why_focus: Practice using the scale, and converting each side before finding area.

problems.text: A real 36-ft boat is 8 in. long in a scale drawing. 1 in. = how many feet?
hints: Scale means real size ÷ drawing size.
You want feet for ONE inch.
problems.why_focus: Practice using the scale, and converting each side before finding area.

problems.text: A logo drawing is 6 in. long at a scale of 1 in. = 5 ft. You redraw it 10 in. long. What is the new scale (feet per inch)?
steps: New scale: 30 ft ÷ 10 in. = 3 ft per inch.
problems.why_focus: Practice using the scale, and converting each side before finding area.

problems.text: Map scale: 1 in. = 25 miles. Two towns are 3 1/2 in. apart on the map. How many real miles apart are they?
problems.why_focus: Practice using the scale, and converting each side before finding area.

2.1.title: Unit rates
2.1.move: Divide to get to ONE, then multiply to scale up.
2.1.trap: Comparing totals instead of unit rates. Making 9 of 25 shots is worse than 8 of 20.

why.goal: Compare deals and speeds fairly by turning any rate into 'how much for ONE.'
why.supports_future: Every skill after this starts with a unit rate: equations, graphs, scale drawings, and later percent and slope.
why.why_you_need_it: Totals can fool you. 9 of 25 shots sounds better than 8 of 20, but per shot it's worse.
why.real_life: Grocery unit prices, miles per hour, steps per mile, pay per hour, phone plans.
why.building_block: Foundation. The first block of the unit; the rest is built from it.

2.2.title: Unit rates with fractions
2.2.move: Keep, change, flip, then cancel before you multiply.
2.2.trap: Flipping the wrong fraction. Only the divisor (the 'per' amount) flips.

why.goal: Do the same 'get to ONE' move when the amounts are fractions.
why.supports_future: Recipes, maps, and scale drawings use fraction rates. Lessons 2.4 and 2.8 depend on this.
why.why_you_need_it: Real measurements aren't always whole numbers: 3/4 cup, 1/6 hour, 2 1/2 miles.
why.real_life: Recipes, speed over a short time, fabric per item, map scales, medicine doses.
why.building_block: Builds on 2.1 plus fraction division from 6th grade.

2.3.title: Is it proportional?
2.3.move: Divide y ÷ x in EVERY row. All the same means proportional.
2.3.hook: Every row, same number, or no.
2.3.trap: Checking only two rows. One row that breaks the pattern makes it NOT proportional.

why.goal: Decide for sure whether two quantities are proportional.
why.supports_future: You can only use y = kx, a straight line through zero, or a scale factor when a relationship is truly proportional.
why.why_you_need_it: Lots of things look steady but aren't: a setup fee, or ages. Checking every row keeps you from using the wrong tool.
why.real_life: Is this a steady price per item, or is there a delivery fee? Phone plans, ride shares, memberships.
why.building_block: Gatekeeper skill: it decides whether the rest of the unit's tools apply.

2.4.title: y = kx
2.4.move: k = y ÷ x. Then write y = kx and use it.
2.4.trap: Using a group price as k. '3 lemons for $1.80' means k = 0.60, not 1.80.

why.goal: Write any proportional relationship as y = kx and use k to find anything.
why.supports_future: y = kx is your first linear equation. Slope, graphing lines, and Algebra start here.
why.why_you_need_it: An equation is a shortcut: once you know k, any amount takes one step.
why.real_life: Pay = hourly rate × hours. Cost = price × quantity. Distance = speed × time.
why.building_block: Turns the unit rate (2.1) into an equation, and sets up graphs (2.5) and slope later.

2.5.title: Graphs
2.5.move: Proportional = a straight line AND it goes through (0, 0). The point (1, k) shows k.
2.5.trap: Calling any straight line proportional. A line that starts at $3 is not.

why.goal: Recognize and read proportional relationships on a graph.
why.supports_future: Graphs of lines, slope, and comparing rates visually in 8th grade and science.
why.why_you_need_it: A picture shows at a glance whether something is proportional and which rate is bigger (steeper).
why.real_life: Charts of cost vs. amount, speed graphs, exchange rates, fitness apps.
why.building_block: Connects the table (2.3) and the equation (2.4) to a picture.

2.6.title: Times or plus?
2.6.move: Decide first: does doubling one double the other? If not, don't use a ratio.
2.6.trap: Using ratios on ages or on 'more helpers means less time' problems.

why.goal: Decide whether a problem is proportional before using ratios, then pick the right tool.
why.supports_future: Choosing the right model is the heart of word-problem solving in Algebra and science.
why.why_you_need_it: Not every steady problem is a ratio: ages add, and more helpers means less time.
why.real_life: Scaling a recipe, splitting work, planning for a crowd, checking a bill.
why.building_block: Mixes 2.1 to 2.5 into one skill: decide first, then solve.

2.8.title: Scale drawings
2.8.move: Make the scale '1 inch = ? ft', then multiply. For area, convert each side first.
2.8.trap: Multiplying the drawing's area by the scale. Convert length and width first.

why.goal: Use a scale to move between a drawing or map and the real thing, including areas.
why.supports_future: Similar figures and geometry in 7th and 8th grade; blueprints and maps in real life.
why.why_you_need_it: Scale is a constant of proportionality: actual = k × drawing. Areas grow by k × k.
why.real_life: Maps, blueprints, floor plans, model kits, enlarging a photo or poster.
why.building_block: Applies y = kx (2.4) in geometry, combining unit rates, fractions, and area.
